source.title: Stress-Testing Capability Elicitation With Password-Locked Models
source.authors: R. Greenblatt; Fabien Roger; D. Krasheninnikov; David Krueger

page_placements.theme: Hidden capabilities (password locks, sandbagging, circuit breakers) recovered by SFT or activation edits

record.file_problem: The paper text is substantially complete. Some figures are represented without their plotted numerical values.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether fine-tuning can elicit deliberately hidden capabilities, using password-locked models rather than models subjected to unlearning.
record.gate_note: The paper cites claims that unlearning may hide capabilities and that jailbreaking can elicit them, but reports no experiments with unlearning, activation edits, quantization, or prompt-only attacks. Its own password-locking and fine-tuning results bear on recovery by fine-tuning. RL results use reward feedback rather than a small relearning set and are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The study does not test any version of the claim. It studies password-locked models, which are fine-tuned on purpose to hide a capability unless a password appears. It then measures whether SFT or RL elicits that capability. No unlearning method (gradient ascent, WHP, RMU, etc.) is applied, so no result shows whether unlearned knowledge is deleted or hidden. The verdict rules exclude studies that induce the behaviour deliberately and don't measure it arising otherwise. Unlearning appears only in related work, which cites WMDP and Lynch et al. as evidence that unlearning may only hide capabilities. The findings are recorded under fits_no_version as an analogous result about fine-tuning elicitation.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct. The authors also note in the limitations and broader-impacts sections that results may be overoptimistic about elicitation ease, because locked capabilities may be more salient than naturally hidden ones.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains models to behave weakly without a password and strongly with one; it does not apply gradient-ascent, Who's Harry Potter, RMU, or another unlearning recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery depends on task and demonstration quality; sample efficiency is lower for MMLU, reference-critique SFT does not reach the with-password ceiling, MMLU domain generalization varies, and RL outcomes depend strongly on weak-policy quality.

fits_no_version.finding: SFT on a few high-quality demonstrations recovers near-ceiling performance of capabilities hidden by password-locking (except code critiques). Demonstrations from one domain generalize to other locked domains.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Capabilities deliberately hidden by fine-tuning-based password-locking are recoverable by small-sample SFT, including from restricted-domain demonstrations.

fits_no_version.finding: Reward-based fine-tuning (expert iteration, iterated DPO) recovers most locked performance when the weak policy explores well, and fails from very weak policies.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: RL elicitation of password-locked capabilities depends on the quality of the starting weak policy.

fits_no_version.finding: In a toy task, models locked from scratch need 2-4x more demonstrations to unlock than models locked via SFT, but still unlock with few demonstrations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hiding installed by fine-tuning is shallower than hiding installed during pretraining, though both are undone by small SFT.

record.problems: The experiments use deliberately password-locked models rather than models after unlearning, and the authors identify several possible disanalogies between password-locking and naturally hidden capabilities. Many plotted outcomes lack numerical values in the text; results report standard errors over 3 seeds.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for each plotted demonstration count or every category/difficulty condition; the text gives aggregate qualitative findings for these sweeps, while individual plotted values are not supplied in the text. Additional sensitivity analyses, including Spanish/ASCII-Math variations and reward variants, are not included because they do not directly test the claim versions.

untested.parts: No unlearning method is applied or evaluated.
No relearning attack is run on an unlearned model; only password-locked models are studied.
No activation ablation or analysis of unlearned models.
No prompt-only attack; the authors say their models are a poor fit for evaluating jailbreaking.
No robust counter-method; self-destructing models are mentioned only as a limitation.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's linking of rows to B treats password-locking as an unlearning analogue, which the version text does not allow. B concerns knowledge hidden by an unlearning method and restored by relearning. Labels were therefore removed. The paper's only bearing on unlearning is a related-work citation of Lynch et al. (an original source) and WMDP.

versions.untested_parts: No unlearning method is tested; the study does not test near-chance targeted accuracy after unlearning, retained general ability, or whether attacks recover no more than on a model that never learned the knowledge.

The study uses high-quality task demonstrations or demonstrations from other models, not unrelated examples or a subset of forgotten facts after unlearning. Its models are password-locked, not unlearned.
No activation direction is ablated, and no analysis tests whether an unlearning method blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
No prompt-only recovery attack is tested.
No robust counter-method to unlearning attacks is tested.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

rows.locator_found: §5.1, Figure 3; intro bullet (MMLU needs a few hundred samples)
rows.problem: Near-ceiling holds for MMLU, but per the intro it needs a few hundred samples; the row states this qualitatively.

relation.reason: Related work discusses unlearning that only hides capabilities (Lynch et al.), but the study's own results are on password-locked models. The reader's 'tests' is too strong.

tranche.reason: Hidden capability is induced on purpose by password-locking fine-tuning, and no unlearning method is applied. The reader's T2 is wrong.

source_check.notes: Password-locked models, not unlearned models. Rows are at most analogies to relearning. Values are figure-only and the rows correctly give none. §7: models locked via SFT unlock 2-4x more easily than models locked from scratch.

statements.correction: Few high-quality demos recover near-ceiling for code and MATH. MMLU reaches near-ceiling but needs a few hundred samples. Code critiques stay well below the ceiling. Single-domain demos generalize perfectly across MATH domains and across Code+MATH. On MMLU generalization varies by domain.
statements.problem: Lists code critiques as the only exception, but the paper says MMLU is not sample-efficient: it needs a few hundred demos, not a few.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Password-locked models fine-tuned on high-quality same-task demonstrations; MATH demonstrations restricted to a domain; joint Code and MATH setting
reader_labels.reason: Fine-tuning recovers correctness close to the with-password ceiling in several tasks, and the reported domain and cross-setting experiments show generalization (r1, r2, r4, r9, r11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Code critiques, MMLU domain transfer, and fine-tuning on Llama7B demonstrations
reader_labels.reason: Critique correctness remains below the with-password ceiling, MMLU transfer varies by domain, and Llama7B demonstrations yield less than ceiling performance (r3, r5, r6, r7, r8, r10).
